raw_response.country: India (Ahmedabad), Indonesia (Bandung, Jakarta), Thailand (Bangkok), China (Hohhot, Tianjin), Taiwan (Taipei), Vietnam (Ho Chi Minh City), Philippines (Manila), Republic of Korea (Seoul), Singapore

criterion_notes.c1: Basic water services (access to drinking water, access to sanitation, and drinking water quality) are included as one of seven indicator categories in the 11-city City Blueprint Framework baseline assessment (p. 4, p. 7, Fig. 3 on p. 8) and discussed descriptively in relation to urban slums (pp. 11-12, Fig. 5), although the paper's overarching focus is integrated urban water, solid waste, and flood/climate management.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper discusses 'water governance' broadly, correlates a 25-indicator composite urban water index (Blue City Index, BCI) with the World Bank national 'government effectiveness' index, and applies a Governance Capacity Framework (GCF) in three cities; however, even on the plain reading, the primary empirical GCF assessment examines governance capacity for flood risk management (in Ahmedabad, Bandung, and Taipei) rather than governance of household or community water or sanitation service access, while slum water/sanitation access is discussed only through narrative commentary on community engagement. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, Criterion 2 is clearly not met ('no'): the study does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure), relying instead on unanalysed macro-governance background indicators, organizational skills/capacity for flood risk, and generic community-involvement commentary.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains empirical evidence: a comparative diagnostic assessment of 11 Asian cities using secondary municipal and national data (Trends and Pressures Framework and City Blueprint Framework, plus 70-city bivariate correlations) and a triangulated desk-study and stakeholder-interview assessment (Governance Capacity Framework) of flood risk management in three cities (Ahmedabad, Bandung, Taipei).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive city-level indicator scores (0-10) for 'Access to drinking water' and 'Access to sanitation' within the 25-indicator City Blueprint Framework (Fig. 3, p. 8; narrative summary, p. 7) and plots World Bank country-level access to improved water sources and sanitation facilities against slum population shares (Fig. 5, p. 12), though its primary governance assessment reports Likert scores for flood-risk governance capacity rather than service access outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: City-level units of analysis and the comparative indicator / stakeholder-interview case-study design are identifiable, but an eligible legal/administrative exposure linked to a water or sanitation service access outcome cannot be identified: the GCF governance assessment addresses flood risk rather than water/sanitation access, and the cross-city correlations aggregate 25 heterogeneous solid waste, wastewater, water quality, infrastructure, climate, basic service, and governance indicators into a single geometric mean (BCI).

evidence_quotes.quote: Second, we analyse the governance capacity to address these challenges of water, waste and climate change in three Asian cities, Ahmedabad (India), Bandung (Indonesia) and Taipei (Taiwan). This paper focusses primarily on ﬂood risk management as the detailed assessments of other water-related challenges in the city of Ahmedabad, Bandung and Seoul are published elsewhere
Each indicator is scored from 0 (much room for improvement) to 10 (best practice), where their geometric mean is called the Blue City Index (BCI).

The GCF provides information on how well different organisations can work together and to what extent capacities are institutionalised. In this way, governance capacity is understood as the result of human skills and expertise.
To minimise the risk of bias and assure diversity amongst interviewees, they were selected according to their roles, expertise and responsibilities.
Figure 5 shows the relation between population living in slums with access to improved sanitation and improved water sources.

raw_response.exposure: Macro-level social, environmental, and financial pressures (Trends and Pressures Index), national GDP per capita and World Bank government effectiveness / climate readiness indices, and city-level organizational governance capacity conditions assessed with respect to flood risk
raw_response.outcome: Composite Blue City Index (BCI) and 25 urban water cycle indicator scores (covering water quality, solid waste treatment, basic water services including drinking water and sanitation access, wastewater treatment, infrastructure, climate robustness, and governance) across 11 Asian cities, plus 27 Likert-scored flood-risk governance capacity indicators in 3 cities
raw_response.population_and_sample: 11 Asian cities (Ahmedabad, Bandung, Bangkok, Hohhot, Ho Chi Minh City, Jakarta, Taipei, Tianjin, Manila, Seoul, Singapore; unit of analysis: city) for the City Blueprint and Trends and Pressures assessments; 3 cities (Ahmedabad, Bandung, Taipei) with local water-sector stakeholder interviews for the Governance Capacity Framework on flood risk; plus 70-city and cross-national secondary comparisons
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the paper includes descriptive city-level indicators of basic water and sanitation access within its 25-indicator City Blueprint baseline of 11 Asian cities and plots country-level slum shares against improved water/sanitation access, it fails Criterion 2: its empirical Governance Capacity Framework analysis in three cities focuses on flood risk management rather than water or sanitation service access, its multi-city correlations rely on unanalysed macro-governance background (World Bank national government effectiveness correlated with a composite IWRM/waste/climate index), and its discussion of slum sanitation/water relies on narrative commentary about community engagement rather than examining any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing service access.
raw_response.study_design: Comparative multi-city diagnostic indicator assessment (11 cities, plus 70-city cross-sectional correlations) combined with desk-study and stakeholder-interview governance capacity case studies on flood risk (3 cities)
